note_on_method: Nobody working on this has played on these courts. Every sentence below is drawn from a Town of Cary page listed in this file, and because the town states its court counts in prose rather than a table, each count is quoted in the town's own words. Where a page is silent — surface at all three, lighting at two of them — the note says so rather than guessing.

slots.description: The Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway is the largest verified pickleball site in Cary and the only one the town describes as lit. Its features list is unusually precise about the difference between its two racquet sports: "Lighted Tennis Court: Reservable 16 hours in advance" sits directly above "Lighted Pickleball Courts: Non-reservable, first-come, first-served". So the sport you can book here is tennis, and the one you cannot book is pickleball — which, counter-intuitively, is the better deal for a player turning up unannounced, because nobody can have reserved the courts out from under you. The count comes from a different page: the park's own entry confirms the courts exist and are lit but gives no number, while the Cary Tennis Park facility page lists this site among its satellite locations as "McCrimmon Park (3870 Cary Glen Blvd.) Six Lighted Tennis Courts and Six Lighted Pickleball Courts". Six is what we publish. The park is a 20-acre site at the south-east corner of Green Level Church Road and McCrimmon Parkway in north-west Cary, opened out of a 2019 parks bond, and the town gave it a nature theme because of the creeks and steep slopes across the site.
slots.getting_there: 3870 Cary Glen Blvd, in north-west Cary. The town publishes no parking guidance for this park — no lot location, no capacity, no time limit — which is a gap worth knowing at the busiest pickleball site in town. Restrooms are listed among the park's features. Paved loop trails run through the site, and there is a community garden that is closed to the public except during events. Note the naming: the town calls this park "Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway" on its own page and "McCrimmon Park" on the Cary Tennis Park page. They are the same place.
slots.what_to_expect: Six lighted courts, first-come and first-served, with no way to reserve them. This is where Cary runs its Monday evening open play, 7 to 9 p.m., and the town's leagues use these courts periodically for match play alongside Cary Tennis Park — so an evening visit may find a league on. Park hours are sunrise to sunset, extended in lighted areas where visitors are taking part in an approved extended-use activity until thirty minutes after it ends or 11 p.m., whichever comes first. Read that carefully: the extension is tied to an approved activity, not to casual play, so lights do not automatically mean a late game. What the town does not publish for this venue is a surface material, whether nets are provided, or any fee — so all three read "Not verified yet" here rather than being filled in with something plausible.

faqs.q: Can I reserve a pickleball court at McCrimmon?
faqs.a: No. The town marks the pickleball courts "Non-reservable, first-come, first-served". The lighted tennis court at the same park is reservable sixteen hours in advance, which is the opposite of what most people expect.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts are there?
faqs.a: Six. The park's own page confirms lighted pickleball courts without giving a number; the count comes from the Cary Tennis Park page, which lists this site as having "Six Lighted Tennis Courts and Six Lighted Pickleball Courts".

faqs.q: Can I play here in the evening?
faqs.a: The courts are lit, and Cary runs open play here on Monday evenings from 7 to 9 p.m. Park hours are sunrise to sunset with an extension only for approved extended-use activities, up to 11 p.m. at the latest, so lighting does not by itself guarantee late casual play.

faqs.q: Is this the same place as McCrimmon Park?
faqs.a: Yes. The town's own park page calls it the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway; its Cary Tennis Park page calls it McCrimmon Park. We publish the park's own name and treat the shorter one as an alias.

slots.description: Ed Yerha Park is the park the Town of Cary points to first: its page opens by saying the park "features Cary's outdoor Pickleball courts, where everyone is welcome and encouraged to play". There are three of them, stated plainly in the features list as "Three pickleball courts", alongside one basketball slab and one open play field. The park was formerly White Oak Park and was renamed for Ed Yerha, a councilmember from 2012 to 2022 who volunteered for the town for more than two decades, helped form Cary's first Senior Advisory Board and made a series of local history videos for the town's 150th anniversary. The old name has not entirely gone: the town's open data still carries the White Oak Park URL on the same map point, which is how we matched the two records to one place. For a player, this is a small, straightforward, purpose-signposted pickleball venue rather than a large one — three courts, restrooms, a picnic shelter, and a town that describes it as the home of its outdoor pickleball.
slots.getting_there: 1216 Jenks Carpenter Road. The town publishes no parking information for this park at all — not a lot, not a capacity, not a restriction — so we cannot tell you where to leave a car, only that the page does not say. Restrooms are on site and the town's status board lists them as open. There is a picnic shelter, available by reservation, and a playground.
slots.what_to_expect: Three courts on a first-come, first-served basis: the town's own status board for the park reads "Pickleball Courts Open - First Come, First Served", and there is no reservation system for them. Come in daylight. The park's hours are published as "Sunrise to Sunset" flatly, with none of the extended-activity clause that Carpenter Park and the McCrimmon Parkway park carry, and nothing on the page states that these courts are lit — so we record lighting as not verified and you should plan for the sun. The basketball slab is listed separately from the pickleball courts, which suggests the two are not sharing a surface here the way they do at Carpenter Park, though the town does not say so outright and we are not going to claim it did. No surface, no nets and no fee are published for this venue.

faqs.q: Does Ed Yerha Park have lights?
faqs.a: The town does not say, so we do not claim it either way. Its page states no lighting for the courts and gives park hours as sunrise to sunset with no extension clause, unlike two other Cary parks. Treat it as a daylight venue until the town says otherwise.

faqs.q: Is this the same as White Oak Park?
faqs.a: Yes. Ed Yerha Park is the former White Oak Park, renamed for a councilmember who served from 2012 to 2022. The town's own page explains the change, and its open data still carries the old name on the same map point.

faqs.q: Do I need to book a court?
faqs.a: No. The town's status board for the park reads "Pickleball Courts Open - First Come, First Served". The picnic shelter is reservable; the courts are not.

slots.description: Carpenter Park is a 16-acre neighbourhood park in north-west Cary whose three pickleball courts share their surface with basketball. The town states it directly in the features list — "Multi-Sport Courts: Basketball & 3 Pickleball Courts" — which is a useful piece of honesty: you are playing on multi-sport slabs, and the lines under your feet are not all yours. The park is also a memorial site, for Flights AE3379 and AE3378, and it holds a central pond with an earthen dam, a community garden, a terraced lawn, preserved forest and pedestrian trails. It is the one venue in this entire directory whose operator tells you how many cars fit, which is why it earns a mention on the city page's parking note that nowhere else in Cary does.
slots.getting_there: 4420 Louis Stephens Drive, and the town publishes "Parking for 30 Cars". That is the only parking capacity any operator in this directory has given us, and it is worth reading against what else is at the park: a playground, a community garden, a picnic shelter, trails and a memorial all draw on the same thirty spaces as the courts. There is a restroom structure on site. No time limit, permit requirement or fee is published for the parking.
slots.what_to_expect: Three courts, shared with basketball, on multi-sport slabs. Expect that sharing to matter — a basketball game has as much claim on the surface as you do, and with three courts a queue builds quickly at a neighbourhood park this size. Park hours are sunrise to sunset, extended in lighted areas where visitors are taking part in an approved extended-use activity until thirty minutes after it ends or 11 p.m. at the latest. That clause refers to lighted areas of the park in general; nothing on the page states that these particular courts are lit, so lighting here is recorded as not verified rather than as present. The picnic shelter at the playground is first-come, first-served rather than reservable. No surface material, nets or fee is published for the courts.

faqs.q: Are the pickleball courts at Carpenter Park dedicated?
faqs.a: No. The town lists them as "Multi-Sport Courts: Basketball & 3 Pickleball Courts", so the three pickleball courts share their surface with basketball and you will be playing over other lines.

faqs.q: Is there parking at Carpenter Park?
faqs.a: Yes, and unusually the town says how much: "Parking for 30 Cars". No time limit, permit or fee is published. Bear in mind those thirty spaces serve a 16-acre park with a playground, community garden, picnic shelter, trails and a memorial as well as the courts.

faqs.q: Can I play here after dark?
faqs.a: Not on anything the town has published. Park hours are sunrise to sunset, with an extension only in lighted areas for approved extended-use activities. The page does not state that the pickleball courts themselves are lit, so we record lighting as not verified. Of Cary's three verified parks, only the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway has lighted pickleball courts stated outright.
